title: Kernel-based guarantees for nonlinear parametric models in Bayesian optimization
claim: Randomized regularized optimization with a nonlinear model concentrates queries at the optimum while uncertainty and regret behave as theory predicts.
layout: 2x3 grid of plots; top fitted snapshots over time, bottom aggregate traces
description: Six matplotlib-style line plots in a 2x3 grid, with sub-captions (a) to (f). The top row has three snapshots of the fitted model at n=1, 16 and 26 observations. Each plots value against x from -1 to 1. A black teacher curve, a green policy network curve, a blue GP mean with a light-blue shaded latent uncertainty band, black observation dots and a red dashed vertical line for the next query appear in each. Over the snapshots the network fit and the GP band tighten around the sharp peak. The bottom row plots individual faint seed traces and a bold mean against observation count (0 to 300). Panel (d) is red optimum visits, rising roughly linearly. Panel (e) is blue GP latent variance on a log scale, falling. Panel (f) is purple cumulative regret, growing slowly. The eye goes first to the top-left legend and the sharp teacher peak.
caption: Empirical illustration of randomized regularized optimization on the finite grid. The top row shows representative fitted-model snapshots at three observation counts, with the teacher, policy network, diagnostic GP mean and latent uncertainty, observations, and next query. The bottom row shows individual policy-seed traces and aggregate means for exact visits to the optimum, auxiliary GP variance at the optimum, and cumulative regret.
abstract: Modern Bayesian optimization and adaptive sampling methods increasingly rely on nonlinear parametric models, such as neural networks, yet theoretical guarantees for such models under adaptive data collection remain limited. Existing analyses largely focus on Gaussian processes, kernel machines, linear models, or linearized neural approximations, leaving a gap between theory and the nonlinear models used in practice. We develop a kernel-based framework for analyzing regularized parametric models trained on adaptively collected data. Our approach uses kernels over the parameter space to induce reproducing kernel Hilbert space structures over the corresponding model class, yielding confidence bounds for models trained with a broad class of regularized losses. We show how these bounds can establish convergence guarantees for approximate Thompson sampling and provide a foundation for analyzing broader likelihood-free Bayesian optimization methods. These results provide a unified route to analyzing nonlinear models in Bayesian optimization and related adaptive optimization settings.
